props.title: College

sections.content: Buster Keaton's College (1927) brilliantly showcases athletic slapstick comedy while satirizing collegiate life and sports culture. Coming after his masterpiece The General (1926), this smaller-scale film demonstrates Keaton's incredible physical prowess and deadpan humor. The film follows a bookish student attempting various sports to impress a girl, letting Keaton display his remarkable athleticism through carefully choreographed failures. It shares DNA with Harold Lloyd's The Freshman (1925), both using academia as a backdrop for physical comedy.

sections.content: The athletic sequences in College demonstrate why Keaton was called "The Great Stone Face." His deadpan expression while attempting pole vaulting, baseball, and track events heightens the comedy through contrast. Unlike Charlie Chaplin's The Champion (1915) which played sports purely for laughs, Keaton's movements reveal his genuine athletic ability even when portraying incompetence. The film's baseball sequence particularly showcases his gift for transforming athletic failure into balletic comedy.

The dark final scene of College, showing an elderly Keaton and his wife dying moments apart, stands as one of silent cinema's most jarring tonal shifts. This ending foreshadows elements that would appear in later works like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Citizen Kane (1941), where comedy gives way to meditation on mortality. The sequence remains controversial but demonstrates Keaton's willingness to experiment with audience expectations. SUBHEAD: Silent Comedy's Athletic Heritage

College belongs to a rich tradition of silent comedians using sports as a vehicle for physical comedy. Beyond Lloyd's The Freshman, Chaplin's The Champion and The Rink (1916) established many athletic comedy tropes. These films influenced later sports comedies from Horse Feathers (1932) with the Marx Brothers to modern examples like Shaolin Soccer (2001).
